newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean opposition blocks spy agency, labour bills.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean opposition blocks spy agency, labour bills.

text.p: South Korean opposition parties on Monday sabotaged government attempts to rush through parliament two controversial bills, one reviving the powers of the once-notorious domestic intelligence agency.

The ruling New Korea Party had hoped to pass legislation rejuvinating the Agency for National Security Planning, Korea's version of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), at an extraordinary session of the National Assembly.
It had also hoped to ram through a labour law giving employers the right to lay off workers and adopt flexible working hours.

About 30 parliamentary members of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics held the speaker of parliament as a virtual prisoner in his office, preventing him from leaving the room to open the session, according to officials at the speaker's office.
Other opposition deputies milled around the entrance to the parliamentary chamber, ready to block the speaker from entering if he managed to sneak out of his office.
It was not clear whether the speaker would try to call parliament into session on Tuesday.
Lee Keung-kyu, a member of the opposition United Liberal Democrats and chairman of the parliamentary labour committee, said opposition groups were demanding more time to debate the labour bill.
"Ruling and opposition parties have different opinions on how and when to discuss the bill, and when to hold open hearings," Lee said.
"We must discuss the labour law in depth and handle it very prudently," he said, adding that the ruling party was intent on rushing it through this year.
Labour unions have threatened general strikes if the legislation is adopted in its present form. They see the law as a threat to near-total job security South Korean workers have enjoyed for decades.

Opposition parties angrily accuse President Kim Young-sam of trying to give sharper teeth to the spy apparatus so it can hound the political opposition, as it did in the past using torture, kidnapping and intimidation.
Kim deliberately weakened the secretive bureaucracy to make good on an election promise.

But the ruling party says the agency must be given wide-ranging authority to meet a renewed threat of subversion from communist North Korea following the incursion of a Northern submarine into southern waters in September and violent leftwing student demonstrations.
The bill would return power to the agency to investigate suspected pro-North Korean activists and people suspected of withholding information on enemy organisations.
Those powers are now in the hands of regular police.
